title: Adani Power Rises 2% After Signing 770-MW Bhutan Hydropower Deal With DGPC
excerpt: The 49:51 joint venture with Bhutan's DGPC will develop the Chamkharchhu-I project on a 30-year BOOT concession, with construction starting in early 2027.
body:
• Adani Power shares gained 2% on Tuesday to touch a day's high of Rs 205 on the NSE after the company signed a shareholders' agreement with Bhutan's Druk Green Power Corporation (DGPC) to develop the 770-MW Chamkharchhu-I hydropower project in Bhutan.
  • The partners will incorporate a joint public company in Bhutan with a 49:51 shareholding (Adani Power:DGPC), initially issuing 4.9 million and 5.1 million shares at Ngultrum 100 per share, with three board seats each and a 30-year concession under the Build, Own, Operate and Transfer model.
  • The peaking run-of-river project sits on the Chamkharchhu River in Bhutan's central Zhemgang district; construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with commissioning targeted within six years of groundbreaking.
  • For investors tracking Indian utility stocks: the deal deepens Adani Power's contracted clean-energy pipeline, but cash flows from the project are unlikely before the early 2030s — this is a long-horizon bet, not a near-term earnings driver.

Adani Power shares rose 2% on Tuesday to hit a day's high of Rs 205 on the National Stock Exchange after the company signed a shareholder agreement with Bhutan's Druk Green Power Corporation (DGPC) to set up the 770-MW Chamkharchhu-I Hydropower Project in Bhutan. The agreement was signed in Thimphu, according to a release filed with the exchanges.

Under the agreement, Adani Power and DGPC will jointly incorporate a public company in Bhutan — with a 49:51 equity split — to undertake the project, India's largest private power producer said. Both partners will appoint three directors each and make additional capital contributions in the agreed proportion as required.

Second Bhutan project under a 5,000-MW ambition

The Chamkharchhu-I project is the second major hydropower collaboration between the two partners, following the 570-MW Wangchhu agreement signed in September 2025. It also forms part of a broader 5,000-MW hydropower development memorandum signed between the Adani Group and DGPC in May 2025.

Located on the Chamkharchhu River in central Bhutan's Zhemgang district, the project is a peaking run-of-river plant — designed to generate electricity on demand rather than run continuously. It will be developed under the Build, Own, Operate and Transfer (BOOT) model, with a 30-year concession running from the date of commissioning.

Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with commissioning targeted within six years of groundbreaking, the company said. The signing ceremony was attended by senior Bhutanese officials, including Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay, underlining the political weight both countries attach to the hydropower relationship.

Winter power for Bhutan, summer exports for India

The project's commercial logic cuts both ways across the border. It is expected to help Bhutan meet peak winter electricity demand — when its own hydropower output drops — while surplus summer generation is to be exported to India.

"We are delighted to strengthen our partnership with the Royal Government of Bhutan and DGPC through the Chamkharchhu Hydroelectric Project," said Anil Sardana, Managing Director of Adani Power, adding that hydropower will play a key role in South Asia's energy transition and that the project would contribute to energy security, lower carbon intensity and shared sustainability goals.

DGPC's Managing Director Dasho Chhewang Rinzin said the project would strengthen Bhutan's energy security, particularly during winter, while creating opportunities to export surplus clean energy to India. Both organizations said they are also evaluating additional hydropower opportunities under the broader 5,000-MW programme.

Why it matters for Indian power investors

For Adani Power, the deal extends a strategy of locking in long-duration contracted assets beyond its traditional thermal base. Hydropower offers decades of low-marginal-cost generation once built, in a grid that increasingly pays a premium for firm, dispatchable clean power. The BOOT structure and 30-year concession give the company a long revenue tail, though the economics hinge on execution over a six-year construction window in difficult Himalayan terrain.

India's demand for Bhutanese hydropower has grown steadily — Bhutan already sells much of its hydro output to India, and the two countries have framed energy cooperation as a pillar of their relationship. For the diaspora watching Indian markets, the project fits a larger pattern: Indian companies are steadily building cross-border infrastructure that ties the region's energy systems together, and Indian utilities are becoming more multinational in their project books.

What's next

Watch for the formal incorporation of the project company in Bhutan and the initial share issuance — 4.9 million shares to Adani Power and 5.1 million to DGPC at Ngultrum 100 per share. The more telling milestones come later: financial closure, the start of construction in early 2027, and progress on the additional projects both partners say are under evaluation within the 5,000-MW programme. The market's 2% move on Tuesday was a nod to the direction, not the destination — the real returns on this one accrue to investors willing to wait a decade.
